theme.q: For the category ‘parent’, having given birth to a child is
o: necessary and sufficient
necessary but not sufficient
sufficient but not necessary
neither necessary nor sufficient
theme.spot: Two checks: must every member have it? Does having it guarantee membership?
theme.why: Anyone who has given birth is a parent, so the feature is sufficient. But fathers and adoptive parents are parents without giving birth, so it is not necessary. The tempting ‘necessary but not sufficient’ is the reverse pattern (like four sides for a square).

theme.q:
Judge these statements.
I. According to the classical view, the boundary between members and non-members of a category is sharp.
II. McCloskey and Glucksberg (1978) found that people disagree with one another about borderline items, but that each person gives the same answer when asked again.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
theme.spot: Check each statement separately against the reading.
theme.why: I is true: with a definition, an item either has all defining features or it does not, so there is no grey zone. II is false: asked twice, two weeks apart, people changed their own minds about borderline items up to 22 percent of the time. They disagree with themselves, not only with others.

theme.q: Shown the same glass, a sommelier says ‘a Pinot Noir’ while her friend says ‘wine’. Which statement is correct?
o: The friend uses the basic level; for the expert, a more specific level has become preferred
The sommelier uses the basic level, because the basic level is fixed by real differences in the world
The friend uses the superordinate level, because laypeople avoid basic-level names for drinks
Both use the basic level, because the basic level is the same for every person
theme.spot: Same object, two people, two levels: who knows more?
theme.why: For most people the everyday middle level (‘wine’) is the basic level. Experts know many distinguishing features, so a more specific level becomes the most differentiated and useful one for them (birdwatchers see sparrows, carpenters claw hammers). The basic level is not fixed by the world: it depends on the knower.
theme.src: [CORE][LO] basic level and expertise; Murphy 4.4 (Tanaka & Taylor, 1991)

theme.q: Rosch et al. (1976) showed participants pictures of objects and asked for the first name that came to mind. The figure shows how many names were given at each level. Which conclusion does the figure support?

chart.title: First names given to pictures (Rosch et al., 1976)

o: The basic level is the default level for naming objects
The subordinate level is preferred because it is most informative
The basic level is the same in every culture
Superordinate names are avoided because children learn them first
theme.spot: Read the bars: which level dominates?
theme.why: 1,595 names were basic level, only 14 subordinate and 1 superordinate: the basic level is the default. The figure cannot show that this is universal; Berlin (1992) found that the basic level shifts across cultures. And superordinate categories are learned late, not first.

theme.q: According to Rosch and Mervis (1975), a sparrow is a more typical bird than an ostrich because a sparrow
o: has many features that are common among birds and few that are common in other categories
is seen far more often than an ostrich, and frequency of encounter is the main cause of typicality
has all necessary and sufficient features of a bird, whereas an ostrich lacks one
belongs to the basic level, whereas an ostrich belongs to the subordinate level
theme.spot: Typicality = how much an item looks like the family.
theme.why: This is family resemblance: typical items share many features with other members and few with other categories. Frequency has some effect but is not the main cause (a rug is seen as often as a table yet is less typical furniture). The classical view cannot explain typicality at all, since every member would be equally good.

theme.q: Rosch and Mervis (1975) taught participants new categories made of items with arbitrary features. Why does this design make their typicality results more convincing?
o: Participants had never seen the items, so everyday frequency cannot explain which items became typical
Arbitrary features can be made necessary and sufficient, so the classical view could be tested directly against them
New categories have no prototype, so prototype theory was ruled out
New categories are always basic-level categories, so the level was held constant
theme.spot: Why build a brand-new category instead of using birds?
theme.why: With new items nobody has an everyday history, so frequency of encounter cannot explain the result. Items with features common in their category were still learned faster and rated more typical, and items sharing features with another category were learned more slowly: both parts of family resemblance hold.

theme.q: Mila has met dozens of fluffy cats and one hairless Sphynx cat, which she remembers vividly. The first time she sees a hairless dog, she immediately calls it ‘a cat’. Which approach explains this best?
o: The prototype approach
The exemplar approach
The classical view
The knowledge approach
theme.spot: Classification driven by a few specific remembered examples.
theme.why: Mila's category ‘cat’ includes the specific examples she remembers. New things are compared with them, so whatever closely resembles the stored Sphynx is called a cat. A prototype is an average built across all members; averaged over dozens of fluffy cats it is fluffy, so it does not predict calling a hairless animal a cat. Close similarity to one well-remembered example deciding the category is the exemplar signature (Allen & Brooks, 1991).

theme.q: Which finding is a problem for exemplar theory but NOT for prototype theory?
o: People know that small birds tend to sing and large birds tend to squawk, and use this to classify
A ‘musical instrument at a campfire’ is more often a guitar than a piano
People ‘recognise’ a never-shown dot pattern from which all studied patterns were derived
Typical members of a category are categorised faster than atypical ones
theme.spot: Which result needs a summary the person never encountered?
theme.why: Posner et al. (1967): the prototype pattern was never shown, so it could never have been stored as an exemplar, yet it was ‘recognised’. Only an abstracted average explains that. Correlated features and context effects are problems for prototype theory, and typicality is explained by both theories.

theme.q: Two groups learn about a made-up deep-sea fish. Group A learns: lives in total darkness, has huge eyes, gives off light. Group B learns: lives in total darkness, has tiny eyes, has bright red stripes. Group A learns the concept faster and remembers ‘huge eyes’ best. Which approach explains this best?
o: The prototype approach
The exemplar approach
The knowledge approach
The classical view
theme.spot: Features that make sense together are easier to learn.
theme.why: The knowledge approach says we link new concepts to what we already know: big eyes and light make sense in darkness, so the concept is coherent. Murphy and Allopenna (1994) found exactly this with the ‘donker’ and ‘blegdav’. Prototype and exemplar theory put no constraint on which features a concept contains, so they do not predict it.

theme.q: Children hear that a goat had an operation so that it now looks and bleats exactly like a sheep, and that a broom was rebuilt so that it now works as a rake. Most say the animal is still a goat, but the broom is now a rake. What does this show?
o: People believe natural kinds have a hidden essence, while artefacts are defined by their function
Children classify by appearance, while adults classify by function
The basic level of animals is lower than the basic level of tools
Animals are classified by comparison with a prototype, and tools by comparison with remembered exemplars
theme.spot: Looks changed, membership did not: a hidden core.
theme.why: This is psychological essentialism, as in Keil's (1989) raccoon-skunk study: a natural kind keeps an invisible essence whatever it looks like. For an artefact such as a coffeepot turned birdfeeder, people accept the change, because artefacts seem to have no essence. Adults and children over four answered alike.

theme.q: Which of the following is an ad hoc category?
o: Birds of prey
Kitchen utensils
Ways to keep a toddler busy on a long flight
A golden cage (said of a well-paid job you cannot leave)
theme.spot: Made up on the spot to serve a goal.
theme.why: An ad hoc category (Barsalou, 1983) forms for a specific goal; its members (stickers, snacks, a tablet) share nothing except that goal. Birds of prey are a natural kind, kitchen utensils are artefacts, and ‘a golden cage’ is a metaphorical concept, the loosest type of all.

theme.q:
The table lists the links in part of a semantic network. Participants see the prime FIRE and then decide as fast as possible whether a target is a word. In which order will the targets be recognised, from fastest to slowest?
Link
FIRE – SMOKE
FIRE – RED
RED – ROSE
CHAIR – TABLE
o: SMOKE, ROSE, CHAIR
ROSE, SMOKE, CHAIR
CHAIR, ROSE, SMOKE
SMOKE, CHAIR, ROSE
theme.spot: Count the links between the prime and each target.
theme.why: Activation spreads from FIRE along its links and weakens with distance. SMOKE is one link away and gets the biggest head start; ROSE is two links away (via RED) and gets a smaller one; CHAIR is not connected at all, so it gets no priming.

theme.q: The figure shows illustrative mean reaction times for correct ‘true’ answers in a category verification task. What would the figure look like if the classical view of categories were correct?
o: The bars would rise even more steeply from robin to penguin
All three bars would be about equally high
The penguin bar would be lowest, because penguins are distinctive
The chicken bar would be highest, because it lies on the borderline
theme.spot: Classical view: every member is an equally good member.
theme.why: In the classical view an item either has all defining features or not, so all birds are equally good birds and there is no reason for speed differences. The real pattern, faster for typical items, is the typicality effect, which the classical view cannot explain.
theme.src: [LO A4, B3] typicality in verification; Murphy 4.6; Robinson-Riegler

theme.q:
Judge these statements about the spreading activation model of Collins and Loftus (1975).
I. The activation reaching a node is summed, and the concept is identified when the sum exceeds a threshold.
II. The more concepts are activated at the same time, the more activation each of them receives.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
theme.spot: Each statement is one assumption of the model; one is reversed.
theme.why: I is true: activation is summed at a node and the concept fires past a threshold. II is false: activation is shared, so the more concepts are active at once, the less each one receives. Activation also fades with time and distance.

theme.q: In a feature verification task, people confirm ‘a cat has whiskers’ faster than ‘a cat has lungs’. How does the semantic network approach explain this?
o: ‘Lungs’ is a distinctive feature of cats, and distinctive features are stored furthest away
‘Whiskers’ is more strongly linked to the node ‘cat’, so activation reaches it sooner
‘Lungs’ is checked against all stored cat exemplars, which takes more time
‘Whiskers’ is a necessary feature of cats and ‘lungs’ is not
theme.spot: Speed of verification = distance in the network.
theme.why: In the network a feature that is closely associated with a concept sits close to it (a short, strong link), so activation gets there fast. Lungs are true of cats but weakly associated with them, just like ‘a cat has skin’ in Robinson-Riegler. Lungs are not distinctive (all mammals have them) and are just as necessary as whiskers.

theme.q: Which profile describes semantic dementia, the mirror image of amnesia?
o: Loss of conceptual knowledge, while day-to-day episodic memory is relatively spared
Loss of the ability to form new episodic memories, while vocabulary and concepts remain intact
Loss of drawing and copying skill, while naming remains intact
Equal loss of all memory systems from the start of the disease
theme.spot: Which knowledge goes, and which stays?
theme.why: Semantic dementia comes with temporal-lobe atrophy and a selective loss of concepts and word meaning, while day-to-day memory, fluent speech and reasoning are relatively spared. Amnesia shows the reverse (episodes lost, concepts intact): together a double dissociation between semantic and episodic memory.
theme.src: [LO C1] Bozeat et al. (2003) intro; Murphy 4.7, 4.11

theme.q: In Study 1 of Bozeat et al. (2003), the patients' drawing scores correlated strongly with their naming and word-to-picture matching scores (r between .96 and .99), while copying the Rey figure and Raven's matrices stayed relatively preserved. Which explanation of the poor drawings does this rule out?
o: A loss of conceptual knowledge
A loss of drawing or visuo-constructional skill
Damage to a single central semantic system
A selective, progressive impairment of semantic memory
theme.spot: What do drawing and naming share, and what does copying test?
theme.why: Naming needs no drawing at all, so the only thing drawing and naming share is meaning. And patients could still copy a complex figure, so their hand and eye work. Together this rules out a loss of drawing skill and supports impoverished concepts from damage to one central semantic system.
theme.src: [LO C2][IDQ C4] Bozeat et al. (2003) Study 1
theme.hy: 10 Drawing correlates with naming, not copying

theme.q: Bozeat et al. (2003) classified each visual feature as shared or distinctive, using the drawings of healthy controls. The figure shows the mean proportion of shared features per item for two domains. What does this predict for the drawings of semantic dementia patients?

chart.title: Shared features per item (Bozeat et al., 2003)
chart.note: Values from Bozeat et al. (2003), citing Rogers et al.

o: More omissions for artefacts than for animals
More intrusions for animals than for artefacts
Artefact drawings will gain wrong features, such as extra legs
No difference between the domains for any type of error
theme.spot: Shared features are the ones that can slip into the wrong drawing.
theme.why: Shared features (eyes, four legs) are the ones that intrude into drawings of items that lack them. Animals have more of them, so animals get more intrusions. That is what was found: omissions did not differ by domain, and once distinctiveness was taken into account, domain no longer predicted intrusions.
theme.src: [LO C2][CORE related] Bozeat et al. (2003) distinctiveness analysis

theme.q: A patient with semantic dementia is asked to draw a peacock from its name. Based on Bozeat et al. (2003), which error is LEAST likely?
o: Leaving out the fan of tail feathers
Adding four legs
Leaving out the eyes
Drawing an ordinary, generic bird
theme.spot: Shared features survive; distinctive ones go.
theme.why: Eyes are shared by the whole domain (almost all animals have them), and shared features are the most robust, so omitting them is least likely. The tail fan is distinctive and goes first, which leaves a generic bird. Four legs is a typical intrusion of a shared animal feature.

theme.q: The figure shows approximate mean errors per item for the three patients of Study 2 of Bozeat et al. (2003). What would the figure look like if the patients' errors came from poor visual or constructional skill rather than from lost conceptual knowledge?

chart.title: Mean errors per item (approx., Bozeat et al., 2003, Fig. 3)

o: Errors would be high in all three conditions, including immediate copying
Errors would rise from immediate copying to drawing from name, as shown
Errors would appear only in delayed copying
Errors would appear only for living things
theme.spot: Immediate copying needs eye and hand, hardly any meaning.
theme.why: Immediate copying relies mainly on visual and constructional skill. If that skill were the problem, patients would fail there too, and the three conditions would look alike. Instead errors are lowest in immediate copying and grow as the task needs more conceptual knowledge, especially for the severe patient IF.
theme.src: [LO C2] Bozeat et al. (2003) Study 2, Figure 3

theme.q: In Study 2 of Bozeat et al. (2003), the patients also drew meaningless geometric shapes from memory after a delay, and all performed within the control range. What does this result rule out?
o: That delayed copying of objects is hard for patients only because of poor episodic memory
That the patients have a semantic impairment
That distinctive features are lost before shared features
That drawing from name depends on conceptual knowledge
theme.spot: A control task: same memory demand, no meaning.
theme.why: Delayed copying needs both episodic memory and concepts. Meaningless shapes need the same short-term episodic memory but no meaning. Normal performance there shows that the object errors arise only when meaning is needed, so they are semantic, not a memory-span problem.

theme.q:
Over 18 months, a patient with semantic dementia names the same picture ‘duck’, then ‘swan’, then ‘bird’, then ‘animal’. Judge these statements.
I. This pattern fits Warrington's (1975) view that semantic memory is organised hierarchically.
II. This pattern rules out the view that concepts are distributed patterns of shared and distinctive features.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
theme.spot: Does a fit with one theory exclude the other?
theme.why: I is true: specific levels degrade before general ones, as a hierarchy predicts. II is false: Rogers et al. (2002) damaged a network built only from semantic features and got the same specific-to-general pattern without a stored hierarchy, because shared features are the most robust.
theme.src: [LO C2] Hodges et al. (1995); Warrington (1975); Rogers et al. (2002) via Bozeat

theme.q: Hampton (1979) asked people whether various items belonged to categories such as ‘kitchen utensils’ and ‘vegetables’. What did he find?
o: Members and non-members formed a continuum, with many items only just in or just out
Typical members were judged to be in the category and atypical members were judged to be out
People agreed completely about which items were members
Sinks and sponges were both clear members of ‘kitchen utensils’
theme.spot: Sharp boundary or a gradual slope?
theme.why: There was no clean break: sinks were only just kitchen utensils, sponges only just not; seaweed only just a vegetable, tomatoes only just not, with much disagreement. Atypical members are still members, so the second option confuses typicality with membership. This fuzziness is a key problem for the classical view.

theme.q: Which finding shows that the basic level depends on the knower and not only on the structure of the world?
o: Less industrialised societies name natural objects with words like ‘elm’ and ‘trout’
Of more than 1,600 names given to pictures of objects, 1,595 were at the basic level
Children use basic-level names before superordinate names
Subordinate categories closely resemble their neighbouring categories
theme.spot: Look for a difference between groups of people.
theme.why: Berlin (1992): North Americans say ‘tree’, ‘fish’, ‘bird’, but people who know more about nature use the level of ‘elm’, ‘trout’, ‘finch’. The same world gives a different basic level, so knowledge matters. The other options are true facts about the basic level but say nothing about differences between knowers.

theme.q: What distinguishes the essentialist approach to categorisation from the classical, prototype and exemplar approaches?
o: It is top-down: we categorise by our theory of what something is at its core
It is bottom-up: we categorise by counting visible features
It stores one average member for each category
It requires features that are necessary and sufficient
theme.spot: Similarity of features vs a belief about the core.
theme.why: The classical, prototype and exemplar approaches are bottom-up: an object is a bird because of its features. The essentialist approach (Medin & Ortony, 1989) is top-down: we use a theory about a hidden core, which need not be visible, so categorisation goes beyond perceptual similarity (as in Rips's bird-like creature that came to look like an insect).

m1.q: For the category ‘grandmother’, being a woman is
o: necessary and sufficient
necessary but not sufficient
sufficient but not necessary
neither necessary nor sufficient
m1.spot: Must every grandmother have it? Does it guarantee being one?
m1.why: Every grandmother is a woman, so the feature is necessary. But many women are not grandmothers, so it is not sufficient. A definition needs features that are each necessary and together sufficient, such as ‘woman’ plus ‘parent of a parent’.

m1.q: A toddler calls a poodle, a Labrador and a chihuahua ‘doggy’, but has no word yet for ‘animal’ or ‘poodle’. Which statement fits this?
o: Children learn basic-level categories first; superordinates are especially hard
Children learn subordinate categories first, because they are the most specific
Children start from the superordinate level and work downwards
The toddler uses an ad hoc category built for a goal
m1.spot: Which level comes first in development?
m1.why: ‘Dog’ is the basic level, and basic-level names are the first labels children use (Brown, 1958), the same names adults prefer (Anglin, 1977). Superordinate categories such as ‘animal’ turn out to be particularly difficult for children, and subordinates come later.

m1.q:
Which description fits the structure in the table?
Link
WEDDING – RING
WEDDING – CAKE
RING – GOLD
CAKE – SUGAR
o: A hierarchy of categories in which ‘ring’ is a subordinate of ‘wedding’
A prototype structure in which ‘wedding’ is the most typical member
A semantic network in which ‘wedding’ is likely to prime ‘ring’
An ad hoc category of things needed to organise a wedding
m1.spot: Concepts joined by associations, no levels or members.
m1.why: Nodes joined by links of different kinds (RING is not a type of wedding) form a semantic network. Activating WEDDING spreads activation to directly linked RING, which is then recognised faster: semantic priming.

m1.q: In Study 2 of Bozeat et al. (2003), patients drew items in three conditions. Which matching is correct?
o: Immediate copying: mainly visual and constructional skill; delayed copying: episodic memory plus concepts; drawing from name: mostly concepts
Immediate copying: mostly concepts; delayed copying: visual skill only; drawing from name: episodic memory
Immediate copying: episodic memory; delayed copying: mostly concepts; drawing from name: visual skill
All three conditions rely equally on conceptual knowledge
m1.spot: Order the conditions by how much meaning they need.
m1.why: With the picture in view, immediate copying needs eye and hand. In delayed copying the picture is gone (count to 15), so memory and concepts help fill gaps. Drawing from name gives no picture at all, so it relies most on conceptual knowledge. Errors rose in exactly that order.

m2.q: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of typicality?
o: Typical items are categorised faster
Typical items are learned earlier
Typical items are mentioned first in lists
Typical items have more necessary features
m2.spot: Three are findings; one mixes in the classical view.
m2.why: Typical items are categorised faster, learned earlier, and named first (‘apples and lemons’). ‘More necessary features’ makes no sense: by definition every member has all necessary features. Typicality comes from family resemblance, not from definitions.

m2.q: Which observation is a problem for prototype theory?
o: Atypical members are categorised more slowly than typical members
People know that small birds tend to sing and large birds tend to squawk
Category boundaries are fuzzy, with borderline items
People ‘recognise’ a never-shown average dot pattern
m2.spot: What can a single average NOT store?
m2.why: An average stores how often features occur, not which features go together, so knowledge of correlated features (Mervis & Rosch, 1981) is a problem. Stored exemplars keep it. Typicality and fuzzy boundaries are what prototype theory explains best, and the dot patterns support it.

m2.q: In a semantic network, why is ‘a robin is a bird’ verified faster than ‘an ostrich is a bird’?
o: Robin is linked more closely to bird, so activation reaches the node sooner
Robin is checked against a stored definition of bird, ostrich against remembered exemplars
Ostrich is a subordinate category, robin a basic one
Ostrich is not stored in semantic memory
m2.why: In a semantic network, closely related concepts are joined by short, strong links. Robin is tightly connected to bird, so activation from one reaches the other quickly and the statement crosses the threshold faster. Robin and ostrich are at the same level of the hierarchy, so level cannot explain it.

m2.q: In Study 1 of Bozeat et al. (2003), how did the patients' drawings of artefacts differ from their drawings of living things?
o: Artefacts lost distinctive detail and became simpler and box-like, but rarely gained wrong features
Artefacts gained many wrong features, such as legs on a kettle
Artefacts were drawn as well as by the controls
Artefacts kept their distinctive features while living things lost them
m2.why: Both domains lost distinctive features. Living things also gained wrong, domain-typical features (a duck with four legs), but artefacts rarely got intrusions; they simply became simpler and box-like. Artefacts have fewer shared features that could intrude.

m3.q: A quiz decides whether an animal is a bird by asking ‘Can it fly?’. Why does this fail as a classical definition?
o: Flying is necessary but not sufficient, since bats fly
Flying is sufficient but not necessary, since penguins do not fly
Flying is neither necessary (penguins) nor sufficient (bats)
Flying is necessary and sufficient, but too slow to check
m3.spot: Test both directions with a counterexample.
m3.why: Penguins are birds that cannot fly, so flying is not necessary. Bats and bees fly but are not birds, so it is not sufficient either. A classical definition needs features that are each necessary and together sufficient, and for most everyday concepts none can be found.

o: basic-level, superordinate-level and subordinate-level categories
subordinate-level, superordinate-level and basic-level categories
subordinate-level, basic-level and superordinate-level categories
superordinate-level, subordinate-level and basic-level categories
m3.why: Granny Smith is a specific type (subordinate), fruit is the broad class (superordinate), and apple is the everyday middle level people name first (basic). Watch the order: the list is not given from specific to general.

m3.q: Asked in December to name ‘a song’, many people say ‘Jingle Bells’; asked in July, few do. Which approach explains this most easily?
o: The classical view
The prototype approach
The exemplar approach
The basic-level account
m3.spot: The context makes certain stored examples easy to retrieve.
m3.why: In the exemplar approach a category is a set of stored examples, and the current context makes some of them extra retrievable. A single fixed prototype should not change with the season, which is why context effects are a problem for prototype theory.
m3.src: [CORE][LO A3] exemplar approach and context; Murphy 4.5.2

m3.q: In Study 2 of Bozeat et al. (2003), errors rose from immediate copying to delayed copying to drawing from name, and the severe patient IF made the most errors. The rise across tasks was much larger for IF than for the mild patient DS. In statistical terms, this pattern shows
o: only a main effect of task
a main effect of task and a main effect of patient, but no interaction
main effects of task and patient, and an interaction between them
an interaction, but no main effects
m3.spot: Two effects plus ‘the gap grows’ = interaction.
m3.why: Errors differ by task (main effect of task) and by patient (main effect of patient). Because the task differences become larger as impairment becomes more severe, the effect of task depends on the patient: an interaction. Bozeat et al. reported all three.
m3.src: [LO C2] Bozeat et al. (2003) Study 2, Figure 3
